shots.t: Look at your hand. The calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, the oxygen you just breathed in.
All of it was made inside stars that lived and died long before our Sun was born.
This is the story of one of those stars. Let's call her Stella.
Her life will last millions of years, and we're going to watch all of it.
From a cold, dark cloud... to a blinding explosion... to the atoms inside you. This is the life of a star.
Space between the stars isn't empty. It's filled with thin gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, and tiny grains of dust.
In some places, this gas gathers into giant clouds called nebulae, tens or even hundreds of light-years across.
Inside, they are incredibly cold. Only about ten degrees above absolute zero.
For millions of years, a cloud like this can simply drift.
But then something disturbs it. Perhaps the shockwave from a distant exploding star.
The cloud begins to collapse. Gravity pulls the gas into dense clumps, and each clump keeps shrinking.
As it falls inward, the gas spins faster, like a figure skater pulling in her arms, and flattens into a disk.
In the center, a hot, dense ball forms. A protostar. It glows, but not from fusion. Only from the heat of gravity squeezing it.
For thousands of years, the protostar keeps contracting. Its core gets hotter, and denser.
Until it reaches about ten million degrees.
At that temperature, something amazing happens. Hydrogen nuclei slam into each other so hard that they fuse.
Through a chain of steps, four hydrogen nuclei become one helium nucleus.
But the helium weighs slightly less than the four hydrogens that made it.
That tiny bit of missing mass turns into energy, exactly as Einstein's famous equation predicts. E equals m c squared.
A little mass makes a huge amount of energy. Its outward push stops the collapse. Stella is officially a star.
A star is a constant tug of war. Gravity tries to crush it inward. The energy from fusion pushes outward.
As long as the two stay balanced, the star is stable. Astronomers call this the main sequence, and a star spends about ninety percent of its life here.
Inside, energy from the core has a long journey ahead.
In a star like our Sun, light bounces around inside for tens of thousands of years, sometimes more than a hundred thousand, before reaching the surface.
Near the surface, hot gas rises and cooler gas sinks, like boiling soup. That's why a star's surface looks grainy and alive.
Once light escapes, it races across space at three hundred thousand kilometers per second. The sunlight on your face left the Sun only about eight minutes ago.
Remember the spinning disk around a young star? It's full of gas and dust.
Dust grains stick together, into pebbles, then rocks, then mountains.
Over millions of years, they collide and grow, until they become planets.
Close to the star, it's hot, so only rock and metal survive. That's where rocky worlds like Earth are born.
Farther out, past the frost line, it's cold enough for ice. Planets there grow big enough to grab huge amounts of gas, and become giants like Jupiter and Saturn.
Then the young star's wind blows away the leftover gas. What remains is a planetary system.
Not all stars are alike. The most important thing about a star is its mass. How much stuff it's made of.
Small, cool red dwarfs sip their fuel so slowly that they can shine for trillions of years. Longer than the universe has existed so far.
Stars like our Sun live about ten billion years.
And the heavyweights, ten, twenty, even fifty times heavier than the Sun, burn hot and fast. They shine thousands of times brighter, but live only a few million years.
A star's color tells us its temperature. Red stars are the coolest, yellow ones are in the middle, and blue-white stars are the hottest.
Stella is one of the heavyweights, about twenty times the mass of our Sun. She will live fast... and die spectacularly.
After about ten million years, the hydrogen in Stella's core runs out.
Without fusion, the core shrinks and heats up, until it is hot enough to fuse helium into carbon and oxygen.
Meanwhile, her outer layers swell enormously. Stella becomes a red supergiant.
She is so big that, if she replaced our Sun, she would swallow Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Deep inside, she burns heavier and heavier elements, layer after layer, like an onion. Carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon... and finally, iron.
Each stage burns faster than the last. Carbon lasts about a thousand years. Silicon burns in about a day.
But what about smaller stars, like our Sun? They never get hot enough to make iron.
When a Sun-like star runs out of fuel, it gently puffs its outer layers into space, creating a glowing shell called a planetary nebula. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets.
Left behind is the core. A white dwarf, about the size of Earth, but with roughly the mass of the Sun.
One teaspoon of it would weigh several tons.
It no longer makes energy. It just slowly cools, for billions and billions of years. That is the future of our own Sun, about five billion years from now.
Stella's ending will be very different. Iron is a dead end. Fusing it doesn't release energy. It takes energy.
So when Stella's core fills with iron, the fire goes out.
With nothing holding it up, the core, heavier than our Sun but about the size of Earth, collapses in less than a second, falling inward at up to a quarter of the speed of light.
It crushes into a ball of neutrons only about twenty kilometers wide, and the falling matter rebounds outward. A shockwave rips through the star.
This is a supernova.
For a few weeks, this single star can outshine billions of stars in its entire galaxy.
And in the heat of the blast, even more elements are forged, and flung out into space.
What's left depends on how heavy the core was.
Often, it becomes a neutron star. A city-sized ball so dense that a teaspoon would weigh about a billion tons.
Some spin hundreds of times per second, sweeping beams of radiation across space like a lighthouse. We call them pulsars.
But if the leftover core is heavy enough, nothing can stop the collapse. Not even neutrons.
It becomes a black hole. A region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. Its edge of no return is called the event horizon.
Gas swirling around it heats up and glows, forming a bright disk. Stella's heart has become one of the strangest objects in the universe.
But the most important part of Stella isn't what she left behind. It's what she threw out.
Her supernova scattered carbon, oxygen, silicon, iron and much more, across light-years of space.
That enriched gas mixes into new clouds... and the cycle begins again.
About four and a half billion years ago, one such cloud, enriched by generations of stars like Stella, collapsed to form our Sun, our Earth, and everything on it.
The carbon in your cells. The oxygen in your lungs. The iron in your blood. All of it came from stars.
As the astronomer Carl Sagan said: we are made of star stuff.
Thank you for watching. Tonight, look up. You're looking at your ancestors.
